quests.instruction: Which birds crowd together in a tight huddle on the ice and take turns standing on the cold outside edge?
quests.hint: Everyone gets a turn in the warm middle.
quests.explanation: Emperor penguins huddle to share warmth. They shuffle around, so every penguin gets a turn in the cosy centre.
quests.funFact: Inside a huddle it can be much warmer than the freezing air outside.
quests.question: Penguin

quests.instruction: Pick the animals that live in big herds, where many eyes and ears spot danger sooner.
quests.hint: The more watchers there are, the less any one of them has to worry.
quests.explanation: In a herd, more eyes and ears mean danger is noticed sooner, and a hunter has a hard time picking out one animal.
quests.funFact: A buffalo herd will sometimes surround a hunter and chase it away to rescue one of its members.
quests.question: Buffalo

quests.instruction: Which big cat usually lives and hunts alone, unlike the cats that live in family groups?
quests.hint: It has its own patch and keeps to itself.
quests.explanation: Leopards are solitary. They mark their own territory and hunt alone, while lions live in groups.
quests.funFact: A leopard marks trees with scratches and scent to show the area is taken.
quests.question: Leopard

quests.instruction: In a colony of these insects, workers stand at the entrance and fan their wings to cool the home on hot days. Which insect?
quests.hint: The home is a hive made of wax.
quests.explanation: Honey bees do many different jobs. Some fan their wings to cool the hive, while others collect nectar or look after the young.
quests.funFact: Honey bees keep the middle of their hive at about the same warm temperature all the time.
quests.question: Bee

quests.instruction: Which tiny insects link their bodies together to make living bridges and floating rafts?
quests.hint: They hold on tight to one another, leg to leg.
quests.explanation: Some ants hook onto each other to build bridges over gaps. Fire ants can form a floating raft to survive floods.
quests.funFact: A raft of fire ants can float for days.
quests.question: Ant

quests.instruction: Spot the red insect that gathers in big clusters under bark or in rock cracks to wait out the winter.
quests.hint: They hide together until it is warm again.
quests.explanation: Many ladybugs spend winter in groups in sheltered spots, which helps keep them from drying out.
quests.funFact: Some ladybugs return to the same winter hiding places year after year.
quests.question: Ladybug

quests.instruction: Which ape lives in a troop led by a big male who protects the family and settles arguments?
quests.hint: He has silvery hair on his back.
quests.explanation: A silverback gorilla leads the group, decides where it goes and protects it from danger.
quests.funFact: A silverback often thumps his chest to show strength, which can settle a dispute without a fight.
quests.question: Gorilla

quests.instruction: Which tall pink birds leave their chicks together in a big nursery group, with some adults keeping watch?
quests.hint: A nursery group can hold thousands of chicks.
quests.explanation: Flamingo chicks gather in groups called crèches, watched over by some adults. Each parent still finds its own chick by its voice.
quests.funFact: A flamingo crèche can include thousands of chicks.
quests.question: Flamingo

quests.instruction: Which sea mammals live in pods, and sometimes take turns watching over the young while others hunt?
quests.hint: Everyone in the group helps look after the babies.
quests.explanation: Dolphins live in pods. Adults take turns looking after the calves while the others hunt for food.
quests.funFact: Dolphins in a pod can be heard whistling to each other to stay in touch.
quests.question: Dolphin

quests.instruction: Which small burrowing animal stands on its hind legs as a lookout while the rest of the group feeds?
quests.hint: One member keeps watch for all of the others.
quests.explanation: Ground squirrels often have a lookout that stands tall and watches for danger. It calls out a warning if a hunter appears.
quests.funFact: A lookout ground squirrel may give a loud whistle that sends the whole group running to their burrows.
quests.question: Ground Squirrel

quests.instruction: Which animal works with shepherds, using its natural urge to circle and gather to move a flock of sheep?
quests.hint: Its ancestors were hunters that worked as a team.
quests.explanation: Herding dogs have the instincts of their wolf ancestors, such as circling and stalking. Trained dogs use them to move sheep.
quests.funFact: A shepherd can direct a herding dog with whistles from far away.
quests.question: Dog

quests.instruction: Which giants take turns blowing a ring of bubbles to trap fish, while others herd the fish upward?
quests.hint: A curtain of bubbles acts like a net.
quests.explanation: Humpback whales team up to make a net of bubbles. The fish bunch together, and the whales rise up through the middle to feed.
quests.funFact: Humpback whales sing long, complicated songs that change over the years.
quests.question: Whale

quests.instruction: Name the birds that fly in huge swirling flocks, twisting and turning together to confuse hunters.
quests.hint: The flock moves like a single shape, but each bird is following its neighbours.
quests.explanation: Starlings fly in huge flocks, each bird reacting to its closest neighbours. A hunter finds it hard to pick one out.
quests.funFact: A flock of starlings can have thousands of birds.
quests.question: Starling

quests.instruction: Which farm animal feels safest in a flock and becomes stressed when left on its own?
quests.hint: Staying close to the others is how it feels safe.
quests.explanation: Sheep are flock animals. They feel safer when they are together, so a lone sheep can become very worried.
quests.funFact: Sheep can recognise dozens of faces and remember them for years.
quests.question: Sheep

quests.instruction: Which flying mammals roost in big crowds, hanging close together and sharing warmth?
quests.hint: It sleeps upside down, wedged between its neighbours.
quests.explanation: Many bats roost in large groups. Being close together helps them stay warm and protects them from predators.
quests.funFact: Some bat caves hold millions of bats.
quests.question: Bat

quests.instruction: Find the farm birds that have a pecking order, where each bird knows who gets to eat first.
quests.hint: Everyone in the flock knows their place.
quests.explanation: Chickens work out a pecking order, which decides who eats first. It helps reduce fights.
quests.funFact: The phrase "pecking order" came from studies of chickens.
quests.question: Chicken

quests.instruction: In a wild herd of these animals, the leader who chooses where to graze is usually an experienced mare.
quests.hint: A wise female guides the group.
quests.explanation: In wild horse herds the lead mare chooses where the group goes. The stallion guards the herd.
quests.funFact: Wild horses often live in family groups.
quests.question: Horse

quests.instruction: Which animals gather in crowded colonies on beaches when it is time to have their pups?
quests.hint: They come ashore together.
quests.explanation: Many seals haul out onto beaches in huge numbers to give birth and raise their pups.
quests.funFact: A beach colony of seals can be very noisy, with mothers and pups calling to find each other.
quests.question: Seal

quests.instruction: Name the animal that lives mostly alone, but gathers with others at rivers when salmon are running.
quests.hint: It's a loner, until the fish arrive.
quests.explanation: Bears are mostly solitary. They gather when there is lots of food, like salmon in a river.
quests.funFact: At salmon streams, bears from many different places can end up fishing side by side.
quests.question: Bear

quests.instruction: Pick the striped animals that live in small family groups, which may join into huge herds.
quests.hint: One male leads each family group.
quests.explanation: Zebras live in family groups with one male and several females. Many family groups may join up into a big herd.
quests.funFact: A zebra family can recognise each other by their voices and smell, as well as their stripes.
quests.question: Zebra

quests.instruction: Find the colourful birds that live in noisy flocks, calling to each other to stay together.
quests.hint: A chorus of calls keeps everyone in touch.
quests.explanation: Many parrots live in flocks and call to each other all day, which helps them stay together and find food.
quests.funFact: Some parrots greet each other with special calls, like a name.
quests.question: Parrot

quests.instruction: Which eight-legged hunters usually live alone, because they would eat each other if crowded together?
quests.hint: Most of them only meet to mate.
quests.explanation: Most spiders are solitary hunters. A few kinds do live in groups and share webs.
quests.funFact: Some spiders build webs together in large communities.
quests.question: Spider

quests.instruction: Which clever sea animal lives alone and spends most of its life in a den of its own?
quests.hint: Its home is a hidden crevice.
quests.explanation: Octopuses are solitary. Each one has its own den, which it decorates with shells.
quests.funFact: An octopus sometimes blocks the doorway of its den with stones.
quests.question: Octopus

quests.instruction: Which spiky animal lives alone and meets others of its kind only to mate?
quests.hint: It spends its nights wandering alone.
quests.explanation: Hedgehogs are solitary. They forage on their own at night and sleep alone in nests.
quests.funFact: A hedgehog might visit many gardens in a single night.
quests.question: Hedgehog

quests.instruction: A zebra strays far from its herd. Which animal is most likely to take advantage?
quests.hint: A hunter looks for the animals that are alone.
quests.explanation: Alone, a zebra has fewer eyes watching for danger. Lions often target animals that are lone, young or old.
quests.funFact: Lions hunt most often at dusk or in the dark.
quests.question: Lion

quests.instruction: Which insect can't live for long away from its colony, because the colony works as one?
quests.hint: Each one has a job that the others depend on.
quests.explanation: A honey bee depends on its colony for warmth, food and safety. A lone bee away from the hive doesn't survive for long.
quests.funFact: A honey bee colony works so closely together that it is sometimes called a superorganism.
quests.question: Bee

quests.instruction: Which animals pass skills along by watching each other, such as washing food in water before eating it?
quests.hint: Young ones copy what the older ones do.
quests.explanation: Some monkeys learn by watching. Japanese macaques learned to wash sweet potatoes in water, and others copied them.
quests.funFact: Young monkeys learn which foods are safe by watching their mothers.
quests.question: Monkey

quests.instruction: Which of these animals usually lives in the biggest group?
quests.hint: Its colony can have thousands of members.
quests.explanation: Ant colonies can have thousands, or even millions, of ants. Tigers and bears mostly live alone.
quests.funFact: One giant colony of Argentine ants stretches for thousands of kilometres across Europe.
quests.question: Ant

quests.instruction: Which animal could not do well hunting large prey alone, so it works as a team?
quests.hint: The prey is much bigger than a single hunter.
quests.explanation: Wolves hunt large animals, which is hard for one wolf alone. Working as a pack gives them a much better chance.
quests.funFact: A wolf pack is usually a family: a pair and their pups, and sometimes older offspring.
quests.question: Wolf

quests.instruction: Which of these is the odd one out, because it usually lives alone?
quests.hint: The others live in family groups.
quests.explanation: Wolves and elephants live in family groups, but tigers usually live alone, except for mothers with cubs.
quests.funFact: A tiger mother raises her cubs on her own.
quests.question: Tiger
